concepts.mechanism_summary: The materials commonly used for crosslinking collagen as part of the process of converting animal hides into leather fall into three main groups: mineral tannages, aldehyde tannages, and vegetable tannages. Mineral (chromium) tannages: hydrated basic chromium III sulfate complexes form extended polynuclear coordination complexes containing hydroxol, oxo, and sulfato bridges into which ionized carboxyl groups on collagen enter readily as coordinating ligands, accomplishing crosslinking. Chromium forms binuclear complexes that coordinate with carboxyl groups of aspartic and glutamic acid residues in collagen at pH 3.8-4.0, bridging two peptide chains. Aldehyde tannages: aldehyde condensation reactions with collagen amino groups give alpha-hydroxyamines which condense with other collagen amine groups to effect crosslinking. Vegetable tannages: complex, high molecular weight polyhydroxy compounds stabilize collagen primarily via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic bonding rather than true crosslinking.

concepts.mechanism_summary: Sourdough fermentation involves sequential ecological succession of microbial communities. Three LAB genera—Weissella, Pediococcus, and Lactobacillus—are successively detected in sourdough subcultures. Six distinct stages are identifiable over 14 days: bacterial diversity peaks days 2-6 as taxa shift from opportunistic/generalist bacteria associated with flour inputs toward specialized climax bacterial communities (days 10-14) characterized by acid-tolerant taxa. pH is the key driver: as LAB produce lactic and acetic acids, pH falls from near-neutral to ~3.5-4.0, which selectively disadvantages acid-sensitive generalists and favors acid-tolerant specialists. Flour microbiota is the major driver of strain identity within the climax community.

concepts.mechanism_summary: Two main preservation mechanisms operate in smoking and curing. (1) Dehydration: heat from smoking reduces moisture content, lowering water activity so bacteria and other microorganisms cannot grow. (2) Antimicrobial chemical deposition: smoke contains compounds including phenolics, formaldehyde, and carbolic acid that deposit on food surfaces and directly inhibit microbial growth and mold. A physical barrier effect also occurs as smoke compounds seal the outer layer of food. Curing uses salt/brine osmotically: high NaCl concentrations create hypertonic environments causing water efflux from microbial cells, inhibiting growth. Smoking is frequently combined with salt curing for additive preservation.

concepts.mechanism_summary: Repoussé is a metalworking technique in which a malleable metal is shaped by hammering from the reverse side to create a design in low relief. Chasing is the complementary operation: refining the design from the front by sinking the metal. There is no loss of material—the metal is not cut but pushed into shape in small increments. The word repoussé is French meaning 'pushed up'. Metals harden during hammering (work hardening), becoming stiffer; annealing (gentle heating) can reverse this to restore malleability. The result is three-dimensional relief form created entirely through the redistribution of metal volume by controlled plastic deformation.

atoms.verbatim_quote: There is no loss of material when forming metal with these techniques - the metal is not cut by the tools but pushed into shape in small increments
atoms.mechanism_atom: Volume-conserving deformation: all material remains; shape change is achieved by displacing metal from low-priority zones to high-relief zones through sequential local pressure

atoms.verbatim_quote: Repoussé refers to pushing the metal out from the back side of the piece - chasing is pushing the metal down from the front. There is a lot of back and forth between repoussé and chasing when creating a relief
atoms.mechanism_atom: Bidirectional iterative refinement: opposed operations (push out / push in) are applied alternately from complementary directions to converge toward the target form

atoms.verbatim_quote: Many metals harden and become brittle as they are deformed by the hammering, which is a phenomenon known as work hardening
atoms.mechanism_atom: Progressive deformation increases material resistance in deformed regions, creating a self-limiting process that requires periodic annealing to restore workability

concepts.mechanism_summary: A catenary arch adopts the shape of an inverted catenary curve—the natural curve formed by a flexible chain or cable suspended from its endpoints under uniform gravity. When the centerline of an arch follows the inverted catenary, the arch endures almost pure compression with no significant bending moment under self-weight. This is because in a hanging chain all forces are tensile acting along the line of the curve; when inverted, these become purely compressive forces along the same line. The form is funicular: forces align with the structure's axis, eliminating shear and bending. Robert Hooke (1675) identified this as the 'true mathematical and mechanical form' for ideal arches.

atoms.verbatim_quote: when the centerline of an arch is made to follow the curve of an up-side-down catenary, the arch endures almost pure compression, in which no significant bending moment occurs inside the material
atoms.mechanism_atom: Shape is chosen such that all loads are directed along the structural axis, converting potentially destructive bending into pure axial compression that masonry can resist

atoms.verbatim_quote: In a hanging chain, the forces are those of tension, acting purely along the line of the curve. When this curve is inverted to create an arch, these tensile forces are transformed into compressive forces
atoms.mechanism_atom: Duality principle: the optimal tension form (hanging chain) is the geometric inverse of the optimal compression form (arch)—same curve serves both modes by inversion

concepts.mechanism_summary: A corbel arch is constructed by offsetting successive horizontal courses of stone (or brick) beginning at the springline of walls so they project towards the archway's center, until projections meet. Unlike true arches, corbelled arches are built of horizontally laid stones, not wedge-shaped voussoirs converging toward a central keystone. Corbelling relies on each stone acting as a counterweight for the ones around it, with thickened walls and abutment fill counteracting gravity's tendency to collapse each side inward. Not all tensile stresses caused by the superstructure's weight are transformed into compressive stresses—the structure retains bending moments and shear at the corbels. It is sometimes termed a 'false arch' because it is not entirely self-supporting without substantial abutment mass.

atoms.verbatim_quote: constructed by offsetting successive horizontal courses of stone (or brick) beginning at the springline of the walls so that they project towards the archway's center
atoms.mechanism_atom: Each course incrementally overhangs the one below; the gap is closed by bilateral inward projection from both walls without any apex element
